## Overview {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## Questions this lesson answers

- How do you find a gene in Ensembl and read its Gene tab?
- What is the difference between all annotated transcripts, protein-coding transcripts, and the MANE Select transcript?
- Where do phenotype, disease, and Gene Ontology annotations appear, and where do they come from?
- How do you inspect exons, untranslated regions, cross-references, and expression probes for a single transcript?
- How do you start from a disease and work back to a gene?
- How do you navigate, configure, and export a genomic region?
- How do you read allele frequencies, ancestral alleles, and conservation for a SNP?
- How do you predict the consequences of a structural variant with VEP?
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this session you should be able to:

1. Search Ensembl by gene name, by phenotype, and by genomic coordinates.
2. Choose an appropriate transcript for downstream work, and justify the choice.
3. Turn browser tracks on and off, and export sequence in FASTA format.
4. Interpret population genetics, conservation, and phenotype association data for a variant.
5. Run the Variant Effect Predictor on a structural variant and filter the results.
:::

| | |
|---|---|
| **Time estimate** | ~1.5 hours (5 exercises, roughly 15 to 20 minutes each) |
| **Level** | Introductory |
| **Prerequisites** | Genes, transcripts, exons, UTRs, and the idea of a reference genome |
| **Software needed** | A web browser only |

: Practical details {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple"}
Ensembl publishes a new release several times a year, and annotation changes
between releases. Transcript counts, transcript names, identifier versions, and
even the set of associated phenotypes may differ from the answers given here.
Treat any mismatch as a discussion point rather than a mistake: ask students
which release they are looking at, and where that information is displayed on
the page.
:::

## Exploring the MYH9 gene in human {#sec-myh9}

`MYH9` encodes myosin heavy chain 9, a non-muscle myosin.

### Locating the gene {#sec-myh9-locate}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

1. Go to <https://www.ensembl.org>.
2. Select **Human** from the species drop-down list.
3. Type `MYH9` in the search box and click **Go**.
4. Click **MYH9 (Human Gene)** in the results to land on the **Gene** tab.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Which chromosome and which strand is the gene on?
2. How many transcripts (splice variants) are annotated, and how many are protein coding?
3. Which is the longest protein-coding transcript, and how long is the protein it encodes?
4. Which transcript would you take forward for further study, and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Chromosome 22, on the reverse strand.
2. 23 transcripts, of which 6 are protein coding.
3. MYH9-215, encoding a protein of 1,981 amino acids.
4. MYH9-201, because it is the **MANE Select** transcript. MANE Select
   transcripts are agreed between Ensembl and RefSeq as the single
   representative transcript for a gene, with matching sequences in both
   databases, which makes results easier to compare across resources. Hover
   over the MANE Select flag in the transcript table for the definition.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why "longest" and "best" are not the same thing

Note that the longest protein-coding transcript (MYH9-215) is not the one we
choose to work with. Length is a poor proxy for biological relevance. 

Ask yourself: What would you do if a gene had no MANE Select transcript? What
evidence should you look for instead? (Hint: look at the expression support, protein evidence, TSL, and APPRIS flags in the transcript table).
:::

### Phenotypes {#sec-myh9-phenotypes}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

1. Click **Phenotypes** in the left-hand panel.
2. The table is long. Type `MIM` in the filter box at the top right to keep only
   entries from Mendelian Inheritance in Man.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

Are any diseases associated with this gene according to MIM?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Yes, several. Two examples are deafness (autosomal dominant 17) and
macrothrombocytopenia with granulocyte inclusions, with or without nephritis
or sensorineural hearing loss. Click any record for more detail.
:::
::::

### Gene Ontology {#sec-myh9-go}

The Gene Ontology project annotates gene products in three separate namespaces:
biological process, cellular component, and molecular function.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

Click **GO: Biological process** in the left-hand panel.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

What functions is MYH9 annotated with?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Angiogenesis, cell adhesion, and protein transport are among the biological
processes listed. Note that all of the GO terms here are attached to a single
transcript, ENST00000216181.
:::
::::

### Inside one transcript {#sec-myh9-transcript}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

1. In the transcript table, click the transcript ID for **MYH9-201**
   (ENST00000216181) to move to the **Transcript** tab.
2. Click **Exons** in the left-hand panel.
3. Then click **General identifiers** in the left-hand panel.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. How many exons does this transcript have?
2. Are any exons completely or partially untranslated?
3. Is there a matching sequence in UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. 41 exons, as reported in the transcript summary.
2. Exon 1 is completely untranslated, and exons 2 and 41 are partially
   untranslated. UTR sequence is shown in orange. The **cDNA** view in the
   left-hand panel shows the same thing in sequence form.
3. Yes: P35579.254 in UniProt/Swiss-Prot matches the translation of this
   Ensembl transcript. Click the accession to jump to UniProtKB, or click
   **align** to see the alignment.
:::
::::

## Finding a gene associated with a phenotype {#sec-pah}

Phenylketonuria is a genetic disorder in which phenylalanine cannot be
metabolised in any body tissue. Phenylalanine accumulates, causing seizures and
intellectual disability. Here we work in the opposite direction to the previous
exercise: from the disease to the gene.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

1. Go to the Ensembl homepage.
2. Type `phenylketonuria` in the search box and click **Go**.
3. Narrow the results to **Gene** using the left-hand menu.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

Which gene is associated with this disorder?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
`PAH`, phenylalanine hydroxylase, ENSG00000171759.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: compare the transcripts

1. If the transcript table is hidden, click **Show transcript table**.
2. Click **Transcript comparison** in the left-hand menu.
3. Click **Select transcripts**, then either tick each protein-coding transcript
   in turn or use the drop-down and choose **Protein coding**.
4. Close the menu to see the comparison.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

How many protein-coding transcripts does PAH have?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Six.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: cross-references and structure

1. Click **External references** in the left-hand menu.
2. Then open the transcript table, click the MANE Select ID
   (ENST00000553106.6), and choose **PDB 3D protein model** in the left-hand
   menu.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. What is the MIM gene identifier for PAH?
2. In the model `2pah`, how many protein molecules can you see?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}

1. 612349.
2. Two. The model `2pah` is shown by default; rotate it if the second chain is
   not obvious at first.
:::
::::

## Exploring a genomic region {#sec-region}

This exercise moves from gene-centric to coordinate-centric browsing.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: navigate to the region

1. Go to the Ensembl homepage and select **Human**.
2. Type the coordinates in the search box and click **Go**:

   ```
   13:32264000-32492000
   ```
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. On which cytogenetic band does this region sit?
2. How many contigs make up this part of the assembly?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Band q13.1.
2. Three, shown by the alternating light and dark blue bars in the **Contigs**
   track. A contig is a contiguous stretch of sequence assembled from direct
   sequencing information alone.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: zoom in on BRCA2

Drag a box with the mouse around the BRCA2 transcripts, then choose
**Jump to region** from the pop-up menu.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: add the LTR repeat track

1. Click **Configure this page** in the side menu, or the cog wheel icon at the
   top left of the lower image.
2. Go to **Repeats** in the left-hand menu and select **LTR**.
3. Click the (i) button to read the track information.
4. Save and close with ✓, or by clicking outside the pop-up.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Which tool was used to annotate the LTRs?
2. How many LTRs fall within BRCA2, and do any overlap exons?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. RepeatMasker.
2. Ten LTRs overlap BRCA2, and none of them overlaps an exon.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: export the sequence

1. Click **Export data** in the side menu.
2. Leave the defaults (FASTA sequence should already be selected) and click
   **Next**.
3. Click **Text**.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

What information does the FASTA header carry?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
The assembly, the sequence type, the chromosome, the start and end
coordinates, and the strand. For example:

```
>13_dna:chromosome_chromosome:GRCh38:13:32311910:32405865:1
```

This is worth dwelling on: coordinates are meaningless without an assembly
version, and a FASTA file that does not record one is a liability in any
project.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: tidy up

Click **Configure this page**, then **Reset configuration**, then ✓. This turns
off every track you added, so the next exercise starts from the default view.
:::

## Population genetics and phenotype data {#sec-snp}

The SNP `rs1738074`, in the 5' UTR of the human `TAGAP` gene, has been reported
as a genetic risk factor for several diseases.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: find the variant

There is more than one route. Either:

- open the **Variation table** for the human TAGAP gene and use the
  **Consequence** filter to keep only 5' UTR variants, or
- search Ensembl directly for `rs1738074`.

Once you are on the **Variant** tab, click **Genes and regulation** in the menu.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

In which transcripts is this SNP found?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
In four transcripts of TAGAP. It is also an intron variant of one lncRNA
transcript of TAGAP-AS1.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: allele frequencies

Click **Population genetics** in the left-hand panel (or click **Explore this
variant** and then the Population genetics icon).
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

What is the least frequent genotype in the Yoruba (YRI) population from
1000 Genomes phase 3?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
CC, at a frequency of 5.6%.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: conservation

1. Click **Phylogenetic context** in the left-hand panel.
2. Click **Select an alignment**, open **Multiple alignments**, choose
   **91 eutherian mammals EPO-Extended**, and click **Apply**.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. What is the ancestral allele, and how was it determined?
2. Is it conserved across the eutherian mammals?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. The ancestral allele is T, inferred from the alignment in primates.
2. The view centres the SNP (highlighted in red) with its flanking sequence.
   The T allele is conserved in all but two of the eutherian mammals shown.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: phenotype associations

Click **Phenotype data** in the left-hand panel.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

Which diseases is this SNP associated with, and are risk alleles reported?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Multiple sclerosis, celiac disease, and white blood cell count. Risk alleles
and the corresponding P values are given for all three.

Watch the strand. The allele A is reported as associated with celiac disease,
and G appears for multiple sclerosis, yet Ensembl lists the alleles for this
variant as T/C. Ensembl always reports alleles on the forward strand, so the
original publications must have reported theirs on the reverse strand. This is
a common and easily missed source of error when combining variant data from
different sources.
:::
::::

## VEP analysis of a structural variant {#sec-vep}

A breast cancer sample carries a genomic deletion, described here in VCF
format:

```default
13	32307062	sv1	.	<DEL>	.	.	SVTYPE=DEL;END=32908738
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: run VEP

1. Click **VEP** at the top of any Ensembl page and open the web interface.
2. Check that the species is **Human**.
3. Give the job a descriptive name, for example `Patient deletion exercise`.
   Naming jobs is a good habit: it is how you tell results apart later, and the
   name is what appears in the browser when you view the data.
4. Paste the variant into the **Paste data** field and click **Run**.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

How many genes are affected?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Twelve.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: filter the results

At the top of the results table, add the filter **Consequence is
transcript_ablation** and click **Add**.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

Does the deletion remove any complete transcripts?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Yes. Complete transcripts are lost for PDS5B, N4BP2L1, BRCA2, RNY1P4, IFIT1P1,
ATP8A2P2, N4BP2L2, and N4BP2L2-IT2, plus one gene with no official symbol,
ENSG00000212293.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: view it in the browser

Click the location link in the results table, `13:32307062-32908738`. This opens
**Region in detail** in a new tab. If you named the job, the data appears
automatically in red. If not, use **Configure this page** and add it under the
**Personal data** tab.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

You saw part of this region already in @sec-region. What does the deletion do to
BRCA2, and why might that matter in a breast cancer sample?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
The deletion spans the whole of BRCA2, so the gene is lost entirely rather than
altered. BRCA2 is a tumour suppressor involved in homologous recombination
repair, so complete loss is a far more consequential event than a single
missense change, and it is the kind of variant that a SNV-focused pipeline can
easily miss.

This question is an addition to the original exercise set; drop it if you are
short of time.
:::
::::

## Key points {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Take home messages

- Ensembl can be entered from three directions: a gene name, a phenotype, or a
  set of coordinates. All three converge on the same annotation.
- A gene usually has many transcripts. Pick one deliberately, and prefer MANE
  Select where it exists.
- Left-hand panel links (Phenotypes, GO, Exons, General identifiers, Oligo
  probes) are where the cross-references live.
- Genomic coordinates mean nothing without an assembly version, and alleles mean
  nothing without a strand.
- VEP scales the same reasoning up from single bases to structural variants, and
  its consequence filters are how you find the events that matter.
:::

## Exercises to extend the session {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Suggested follow-up

1. Repeat the first exercise for a gene of your own choosing and report the
   transcript you would take forward, with reasons.
2. Take P35579 from the MYH9 General identifiers page into the UniProt lesson
   and compare what each database tells you about the same molecule.
3. Use BioMart to export the exon coordinates of all protein-coding transcripts
   of PAH as a TSV file.
4. Construct a VCF line for a deletion of your own and predict, before running
   VEP, which consequence terms it should return.
:::
